newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu accuses Arabs of "ganging up" on Israel.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu accuses Arabs of "ganging up" on Israel.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Arab states on Monday of ganging up on Israel but called the notion that they could revive the Arab boycott "absurd".

The Arab League, angry at Netanyahu's construction of a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, urged in a meeting in Cairo on Sunday suspending normalisation with Israel and reviving the economic boycott.

"What is required on the Arab side is to recognise that we are not always going to have agreement with Israel but that we don't go back to this mode of 'ganging up' on Israel and making these absurd ideas that the boycott will be reinstated," Netanyahu told Israel Radio's English news.
"Israel has known periods of Israel-bashing more than once and we've been able to overcome it," he said.

In a 12th straight day of West Bank violence spurred by the settlement building, Israeli troops firing rubber bullets shot and wounded two Palestinians during a clash near Jenin with about 200 stone-throwing protesters.

The Palestinian Health Ministry said that as of Sunday night Israel had killed one Palestinian, wounded 14 with live bullets and 195 with rubber bullets, and caused 298 to be treated for inhalation of teargas.

And in a move assailed by human rights activists as collective punishment, Israel on Monday flattened the West Bank family home of a Palestinian suicide bomber who killed three Israeli women at a Tel Aviv cafe on March 21.
The suicide attack and the groundbreaking this month for the settlement, coupled with daily clashes, have plunged Israel's relations with the Arabs into crisis.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy slammed the Arab League decision as part of a bid to topple Netanyahu's government since it came to power nine months ago.
"The peace process doesn't tolerate and will not tolerate an atmosphere of violence -- not on the ground and not in diplomatic violence," Levy told reporters.
Israel's central bank governor Jacob Frenkel declined comment on the revived boycott threat but termed its end one of the key benefits Israel had reaped in five years of peacemaking.
"It can't be reinstated," Netanyahu said of the boycott. "We live in an open world. The economic ties flow. Israel is a technological power with many, many ties with many countries."

Arab foreign ministers said the league draft would put an end to the tentative gestures of Arab countries such as Morocco, Tunisia, Oman and Qatar towards Israel since the Jewish state's first agreement with the Palestinians in 1993.
"The decision was clear and obvious -- to put on the correct line the peace process," President Yasser Arafat told reporters in the Palestinian-ruled Gaza Strip.
Palestinians complain the settlement of 6,500 houses for Jews pre-empts the results of final peace talks yet to come on the status of East Jerusalem, which each side claims as its own.
Arafat's Palestinian Authority said it was rejecting a U.S. effort to get it to restore security coordination with Israel. It said such cooperation was linked to other peacemaking issues.
Egypt and Jordan, the two states which could have the greatest impact on the league action, appeared to be exempt because of their treaties with Israel.

But Netanyahu, asked about Egypt's role in the league draft, said: "The fact that they are time and time again taking initiatives which seek to roll back the normalisation, roll back the peace of other countries is a severe disappointment to all of us who had believed that the Egyptian-Israeli peace would serve as a beacon to other states."
